doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Cab Calloway's band: road, arrangers and shows
title: Six months at the Cotton Club and recording on the side despite Cab's ban
summary: Cab did not want his men recording with others, but Ben Webster threatened to leave, so Hinton made sessions with Teddy Wilson and Billie Holiday.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well in that band you did an enormous amount of traveling. What was travel like with the band?
It was as best it possibly could be at that time. He was insisting… Cab Calloway… first we do six months in the Cotton Club, which is a long time.
To just sit down and just play.
Just sit down [unintelligible] and this is when we got a chance to make some records with whoever was in town, Billie Holiday or whatnot. Teddy Wilson and I were friends from Chicago.
Just on that point now, making records was different somewhat.
Well it was different because they were singles, you just made a single side. It was a single side. But Cab Calloway didn‟t want anybody in his band to be making records with other people.

Ben Wilson was in the band then and Ben… Teddy Wilson and Ben were friends and we were friends, so if there‟s a recording session with Billie Holiday, Teddy Wilson calls Ben and I to make it. Well Cab heard about it and he performed. He said, “I am not going to have the guys in my band making somebody else great”. So Ben had a lot of clout because he was a star budding, getting bigger all the time. Ben said, “Well if I can‟t make records with other people I might as well leave this band and get out of here”. Cab didn‟t want that. The next thing I hear, he said, “I‟m glad we‟ve got guys in our band that everybody else wants” [laughter]. So then we would get kind [unintelligible] record and make records. But it was good. There were just a few things like that. We made records on the side with Ben or with Billie Holiday, another lady, I can‟t… the name escapes me now. And of course Lionel Hampton, [unintelligible] go to school. Now the days with Benny Goodman, we made recordings down at RCA. He had [unintelligible] Dizzy, and Al Core, and Hawkins.
Some of those are really big standards now.
